title: Cygnus AI - OTEL token flow & runtime observability deep dive
summary: SE-led deep dive on OpenTelemetry token-level traces and runtime metrics. Covered how Redwood emits token-level spans, OTLP exporter options, dashboarding patterns in Grafana/Tempo, integration with on-prem OTEL collectors, and tradeoffs of KV prefix caching, batching and quantization for latency/cost. Action items include sharing a sample OTLP exporter config, a token-span dashboard JSON, and scheduling an on-prem benchmark with their infra team.
action_items: Alex Kim: share sample OTLP exporter config + collector helm values by 2026-01-23
Priya Shah: export Grafana dashboard JSON for token-span tracing and per-model token-rate panel by 2026-01-22
Daniel Park (Cygnus): provide test model + sample prompt set and access to dev VPC for on-prem benchmark by 2026-01-27
next_steps: Redwood to send security docs + OTLP config
Schedule 2-hour on-prem benchmark with Cygnus infra team
Follow up call to review benchmark results and tuning recommendations
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-20
Start: 14:21 PST   Duration: ~53 mins
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (Redwood Solutions Eng); Jordan Lee (CTO - Cygnus), Marisol Vega (SRE), Daniel Park (ML Eng), Aisha Rahman (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): SE walked through token-level OTEL trace design and how runtime emits spans for each generated token; discussed OTLP collector topology for on-prem, and recommended dashboards and alerts for token latency skew.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Alex Kim: ok, good morning everyone, thanks for carving out time. um Jordan, you wanted an OTEL-focused look at how we emit token-level traces?
[00:00:14] Jordan Lee: yeah, exactly. we're trying to correlate user request latency back to model internals, like where prefix cache hits are versus kv cache misses and batching delays.
[00:00:23] Priya Shah: perfect, i'll take most of the walkthrough. quick agenda: token spans, metrics vs traces, exporting to OTLP or direct to tempo/loki, on-prem collector patterns, and then a tuning checklist for batching/quantization. sound ok?
[00:00:35] Marisol Vega: yes, please — and also want to surface SLO-level alerts for tail latency, like p95/p99 for token inception and whole-response time.
[00:00:42] Priya Shah: cool. so first, how we instrument token flows: Redwood runtime creates a span at request start, then for generation we create sub-spans per token emission event — so you get per-token timings, kv cache lookup spans (we call them 'kv-lookup' but the recorder sometimes shows kay-vee lookup), and batching/grouping spans. these are standard OpenTelem, sorry, OpenTelemetry spans with attributes: model.name, model.version, seq_len, prompt.id, batch.size, cache.hit boolean.
[00:01:12] Daniel Park: do you actually send every token span to OTLP in production? that sounds... heavy.
[00:01:18] Priya Shah: good call — by default we sample. we have three modes: 1) full token spans for debugging or short-lived trials, 2) tail-sampled token spans where we only export token spans for requests that exceed a latency threshold or have errors, and 3) aggregate metrics only (per-model token counters, histograms). tailsampling is often the sweet spot for production because you capture the problematic cases without exploding telemetry volume.
[00:01:45] Aisha Rahman: and latency: do token spans show the KV cache effect? like is there a separate span for prefix cache?
[00:01:51] Priya Shah: yes — we emit 'prefix-cache' and 'kv-lookup' spans. prefix-cache is an in-memory fast path and usually sub-ms, kv-lookup is our distributed cache lookup for externalized KV. in the traces you'll see batch.wait span, kv-lookup, and token-generation kernel spans. sometimes transcription shows K-V as "k v cache" but the tags include cache.type and cache.node so you can filter.
[00:02:19] Jordan Lee: ok can you show a dashboard mock?
[00:02:23] Priya Shah: sure — showing screen... (screenshare) — top-left is request-level waterfall from Tempo/Jaeger, we map each token span as a narrow bar so you can inspect where the tail happens. to the right there's a per-model token throughput panel (Prom counter per second), bottom is histogram for per-token latency p50/p95/p99 and a KP panel for kv-cache hit rate. we also recommend a derived panel that flags when batch.wait > X ms and kv-lookup > Y ms simultaneously.
[00:03:02] Marisol Vega: what exporter are you recommending? OTLP/gRPC to our on-prem collector? we use the otelcol helm chart.
[00:03:09] Ravi Menon: OTLP gRPC is our recommended path for on-prem. you can also do OTLP over HTTP, but grpc gives better throughput for high cardinality spans. we provide a sample otlp-exporter config in the repo — we'll share it — it sets batching/timeout in the exporter to avoid tailing the request with telemetry flush latency.
[00:03:31] Daniel Park: question about cardinality — model.version and prompt.id can blow up traces. how do you avoid high-cardinality tag explosion?
[00:03:38] Priya Shah: we have two mitigations: we hash prompt.id into a short id for trace attributes, and we recommend mapping model.version to a limited set via a prometheus-style label whitelist. and again tail-sampling helps. also, we expose token-level metrics aggregated by model.name and quantization profile to keep cardinality bounded.
[00:03:58] Jordan Lee: quantization — people talk int8 and 4-bit. what's the impact on token latency variability?
[00:04:05] Priya Shah: quantization reduces compute per token, but introduces variance on first token sometimes due to kernel selection and dequantization steps. in practice, int8 gives consistent gains, 4-bit (nv-llm-ish) can be faster but heavier on tail variance. our runtime tries to select kernels that are quantization-friendly and we emit a 'kernel.selection' attribute to trace which path was taken. that helps correlate poor tails to the kernel chosen.
[00:04:32] Marisol Vega: do you instrument batching? like why would batch.wait sometimes be long?
[00:04:37] Priya Shah: yes — we have 'batching.wait' spans at the request side and a 'batch.exec' span for the collective GPU op. long batch.wait happens when traffic is low and autoscaler hasn't consolidated containers or your burst policy isn't configured. we expose a service-level histogram for batch.wait so you can see the distribution. also if prefix-cache hits are high, batch sizes shrink because responses are fast, which actually can increase per-token cost. it's a tradeoff.
[00:05:05] Daniel Park: VPC/on-prem specifics — we want to keep telemetry internal. do we need to open outbound to Redwood or can we keep everything in our VPC?
[00:05:13] Alex Kim: for Private deployments you keep the control plane separate — but telemetry is configurable: you can push OTLP to your in-cluster collector and then forward to your internal Tempo/Grafana. Redwood can also accept an OTLP pull if you set up a secure peering, but most customers keep telemetry internal and we surface summarized metrics over the private control plane.
[00:05:35] Aisha Rahman: any HSM/KMS considerations for trace data? we redact PII before exporting but still want keys to be handled in HSM.
[00:05:43] Priya Shah: we recommend client-side redaction filters in the runtime before spans leave the host. keys used for encryption of telemetry payloads can be managed by your KMS — the collector can be configured to sign/encrypt to an internal bucket. Redwood's private distro supports integration with customer KMS/HSM for secrets used by the runtime but we don't push raw traces off-prem unless configured.
[00:06:10] Jordan Lee: examples of alerting rules we should add?
[00:06:13] Priya Shah: p99 token-latency > threshold, sudden drop in kv-cache hit rate, batch.wait p95 > x ms, model.kernel.selection change events, and a drift alert if per-model token quality metrics (we use BLEU-ish heuristics for internal evals) degrade.
[00:06:30] Marisol Vega: about dashboards: can you send a Grafana JSON export so we can import?
[00:06:34] Alex Kim: yes, Priya will share the dashboard and an example otlp-collector config.
[00:06:40] Priya Shah: i'll share two dashboards — one focused on token span waterfall and one on aggregated token metrics and alerts. they include panels for prefix cache hitrate, kv latency, batch wait distribution, and quantization kernel mix.
[00:06:56] Jordan Lee: let's talk load testing — we want to see tail behaviour with our VPC infra. what's the recommended setup?
[00:07:03] Ravi Menon: recommend a three-phase test: warmup with prefix-heavy prompts, single-request P95 targeting to capture cold cache path, then ramp to target RPS with steady-state. instrument with OTLP and our in-runtime internal counters exported as Prom metrics so you can correlate per-token traces with infra metrics (GPU utilization, host irq, network).
[00:07:27] Daniel Park: can Redwood's runtime emit Prom counters directly instead of going through OTLP?
[00:07:31] Priya Shah: yes — we can push Prom-compatible metrics to a pushgateway or expose /metrics endpoint. you can scrape it from your prometheus. token counters are aggregated by model and quantization profile, not every token. we expose both histogram buckets and counters on /metrics.
[00:07:47] Marisol Vega: i'm worried about overhead. what's the perf cost of token spans at scale?
[00:07:52] Priya Shah: overhead is proportional to sampling rate. full, un-sampled token spans will add CPU and network egress costs — in our bench it added ~8-12% CPU overhead and increased telemetry egress by an order of magnitude. tailsampling reduced that to near-zero overhead for normal traffic and captured problematic traces. also the runtime uses low-overhead span encoders and a fast in-memory buffer to limit blocking the main path.
[00:08:16] Jordan Lee: in the waterfall view, how do you represent continuous batching? like when tokens from multiple requests share a single GPU op?
[00:08:23] Priya Shah: we create a 'batch.exec' span that is parented by each contributing request through a batch.id attribute. on the UI we decorate each request with an annotation linking to the batch.exec span; you can then see how multiple token spans map into that one kernel call. it's not perfect for all UIs but Tempo and Jaeger can show the batch.exec as a separate bar with links.
[00:08:44] Aisha Rahman: what about microsecond granularity? do you capture that?
[00:08:47] Priya Shah: we capture sub-ms timings when supported by the runtime clock; OTLP timestamps are in nanoseconds but your collector and backend must support it. sometimes exporters coarsen timestamps; we'll note that in the exporter config we share.
[00:09:02] Marisol Vega: any gotchas with OTLP collector in high throughput clusters?
[00:09:06] Ravi Menon: yes, the collector must be sized to handle span bursts. set batching.max_queue_size and max_export_batch_size appropriately. also ensure you don't enable excessive processors that do heavy enrichment in-line — offload enrichment to a sidecar if needed.
[00:09:23] Daniel Park: can Redwood route fallback traces to a cheaper storage for long-term retention?
[00:09:28] Priya Shah: we support tiered telemetry: hot spans go to Tempo/Grafana for 7-30 days, cold artifacts (aggregates or sampled raw traces) can go to S3 or an archive you control. we can provide a retention policy template.
[00:09:41] Jordan Lee: latency budgets — for our customer-facing API we need p99 response < 500ms at 50 RPS. what's your experience for mixed workloads with prefix caching?
[00:09:52] Priya Shah: depends on model size and hw. with 8-A100 dedicated pools and prefix caching on, we routinely see p99 under 400ms for 2-4k token models at moderate RPS when batching is tuned. without dedicated GPUs and on bursty hosted, p99 can spike due to queueing and batch warm-ups. we'll run a tailored benchmark to validate.
[00:10:12] Marisol Vega: security question — can we mask prompt contents before traces leave the host?
[00:10:17] Priya Shah: yes — runtime supports a redaction pipeline that can hash or remove prompt.text and only export prompt.metadata. you can toggle this via flag in the runtime config.
[00:10:27] Jordan Lee: showstopper scenario — we see a sudden kv-lookup burst that doubles p99. is there an automatic fallback?
[00:10:33] Priya Shah: yes — we have policy-driven fallbacks: if kv-lookup latency crosses a threshold, route to a degraded model variant or enable local prefix caching fallback. also we can change batching policy to prefer lower-latency single-request execution. these are configurable via rollout policies.
[00:10:51] Alex Kim: ok we're ~40 minutes in; do you want to go deeper on any piece?
[00:10:55] Daniel Park: can you walk through the otlp-collector helm snippet you mentioned?
[00:10:59] Priya Shah: sure — snippet on screen — it sets receiver otlp.grpc, exporter to tempo with endpoint tempocollector:4317, batch processor with timeout 50ms and max_export_batch_size 512, resource attributes include service.name=redwood-runtime, plus a tail-sampling processor that samples based on latency > 250ms. note: some of those values are conservative; tweak for your cluster.
[00:11:29] Marisol Vega: can you also add a rule to drop prompt.text on exporters?
[00:11:33] Priya Shah: yes the processor chain in the helm snippet includes an attributes processor that removes prompt.text and replaces prompt.id with a hashed id. we'll send the full helm values.
[00:11:44] Jordan Lee: any example queries you use to find correlation between batch.wait and p99?
[00:11:49] Priya Shah: yes — we included a promql example: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model)) and then label_join to correlate batch_wait buckets. we'll include these queries in the dashboard JSON.
[00:12:05] Aisha Rahman: one last infra question: for private deployment, do you prefer sidecar collectors or cluster-level daemonset?
[00:12:11] Ravi Menon: cluster-level daemonset is simpler for scale; sidecar gives better request affinity and local redaction but increases resource footprint. choose sidecar if you need per-pod local redaction with high security requirements.
[00:12:26] Jordan Lee: ok, that's helpful. let's recap and next steps.
[00:12:30] Alex Kim: recap: Redwood will share OTLP exporter config, two Grafana dashboard JSONs (token waterfall + aggregated metrics), and an on-prem benchmarking plan. Cygnus will provide test prompts, dev VPC access, and target SLOs. schedule a 2-hour benchmark next week.
[00:12:46] Marisol Vega: yes, action items sound good. please also include guidance on quantization profiles that minimize tail variance.
[00:12:54] Priya Shah: will do — i'll add quantization notes and kernel selection heuristics in the doc.
[00:12:59] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone, that was super useful.
[00:13:03] Alex Kim: thanks, we'll follow up via the deck and repo links.
[00:13:07] (meeting ends)

References/Links mentioned: repo: github.com/redwood-inference/otel-examples (sample), dashboard export (to be shared), otlp-collector helm snippet (to be shared).

Notes on transcription quality: some acronyms became OTEL/otel/OTLP inconsistently; "kay-vee" for KV cache appears as spoken text. occasional overlap and lost small words.
